title: Generative AI: learning a distribution and sampling from it

items.context:
Data follow y = |x| with a little noise, and there are none for −0.5 < x < 0.5. You fit x
as a straight-line function of y by least squares and ask it which x gives y = 0.75. What
does it answer?
items.why:
Least squares predicts the mean of x given y. Half the points near y = 0.75 sit at
x = −0.75 and half at +0.75, so the prediction lands between them, where there is no data
and no solution. A regression returns one number per input, so it cannot return both.
items.true: About 0, the average of the two answers
false: +0.75, the answer on the branch you happened to picture
−0.75, because the fit is pulled toward negative x
Both −0.75 and +0.75, one per branch

items.context:
Same |x| data. You replace the straight line with a neural network, still trained by
minimizing squared error, to predict x from y. What happens to its answer at y = 0.75?
items.why:
Squared error is minimized by the conditional mean, whatever the model class. With two
branches the mean is between them, so a more flexible regressor reproduces the same wrong
answer. The question, one number for an input with two answers, is the problem.
items.true: It still sits near the mean of the two branches
false: It moves to one of the two branches, since the network can bend
It returns both answers, one per output neuron
It becomes undefined, since the inverse is not a function

items.context:
Which question can a generative model of p(x, y) answer that a regression of y on x
cannot?
items.why:
A model of the joint can be conditioned on any variables. Fixing y and sampling x is an
inverse problem, and the samples include every branch the data support. A regression of y
on x only answers forward.
items.true: Every x consistent with an observed y
false: The expected value of y at a new, unseen x
The gradient of y with respect to each input x
The training error of the fit on the observed data

items.context:
Fitting Gaussian mixtures to the |x| data gives BIC = 543 at K = 1, −697 at K = 2 and
−673 at K = 4. Which number of components does BIC choose?
items.why:
The lowest BIC wins. BIC penalizes parameters, so the extra components at K = 4 raise it
even though they raise the training likelihood. Two components match the two branches.
false: The largest K tried, since likelihood always rises

items.context: How do you condition a fitted Gaussian mixture on known values of some of its variables?
items.why:
Each Gaussian component conditions exactly with the Schur complement formulas. The weights
are updated by the density each component gives the known values, so the result is again
a mixture that can be sampled directly. Rejection sampling (the last option) works in
principle but almost never accepts a sample when the known value is a single point.
items.true: Condition each component exactly, then reweight components by how well they explain the knowns
false: Refit the mixture by EM using only the rows whose known columns match the given values
Keep the single component whose mean lies closest to the known values and sample it alone
Draw samples from the joint and discard every sample that does not match the known values

items.context:
A teammate fitted a Gaussian mixture to rows of (reflux ratio, steam rate, purity) to find
the operating conditions that give a target purity. Now they need the purity predicted for
given operating conditions, and they plan to fit a second mixture for it. What is wrong
with the plan?
items.why:
Which columns are known is an argument to the conditioning step, not a choice made at
fitting time. The one mixture answers the inverse question, the forward question and mixed
ones.
items.true: It is unnecessary; the same mixture conditions on any set of columns
false: Nothing; a mixture can only be conditioned in the direction it was fitted
The second mixture will need twice as many components as the first one
Purity has to be standardized before it can serve as a conditioning variable

items.context: In flow matching, what does the network learn to predict during training?
items.why:
Training pairs a noise sample with a data sample, picks a point on the line between them,
and regresses the network's output onto the line's velocity with mean squared error. No ODE
is solved during training. Predicting added noise is the diffusion formulation, and telling
real from generated is a GAN's discriminator.
items.true: The velocity of a straight line from noise to a data sample
false: The probability density of the data at each point in space
The noise that was added to a data sample at each step
Whether a given sample came from the data or from the generator

items.context:
Every flow-matching training example is a straight line from noise to data. What do the
sampling trajectories, from integrating the learned field, look like?
items.why:
Many training lines pass through a given point at a given time, heading to different data
points. The network learns their average, so paths start slowly and commit to a branch only
partway through. An ODE gives one velocity per point at each time, so no two sampling
particles are ever in the same place at the same time, while the training lines pass
through each other freely.
items.true: Curved, because the field averages the velocities of all lines through a point
false: Straight lines too, because the network was only ever trained on straight lines
Random walks, because each integration step adds a fresh draw of Gaussian noise
Straight, but each one ends at exactly the training point it was paired with

items.context:
You trained a conditional flow-matching model to generate reactor inputs given an output.
Now you need outputs given inputs. What do you do?
items.why:
The condition is an input to the network, fixed when it was trained. Asking a different
question needs a model trained for it. A Gaussian mixture can be conditioned on any columns
afterwards; a conditional flow cannot.
items.true: Train a second model with the inputs as the condition
false: Integrate the same ODE backward from t = 1 to t = 0
Condition the existing model with the Schur complement
Feed the inputs in place of the noise sample

items.context:
You learned p(τ, C_B, dC_B/dτ) for A → B → C in a batch reactor. To find the residence time
that maximizes C_B, what do you condition on?
items.why:
At an interior optimum the derivative is zero, so conditioning on a zero derivative samples
the stationary points. It finds stationary points, not only maxima, so a second condition or
the second-derivative test tells a maximum from a minimum.
false: d²C_B/dτ² = 0
τ equal to the middle of the sampled range
C_B = 0, the root of the concentration

items.context:
Conditioning a Gaussian mixture on r = 0 gives clusters of Peng-Robinson roots at 0.0440,
0.1273 and 0.8143; numpy.roots gives 0.0348, 0.1280 and 0.8147. What is the right next step?
items.why:
The samples are starting points, one per basin. A few Newton iterations against the true
cubic turn them into the exact roots. The generative model finds every basin at once; the
solver supplies the precision.
items.true: Polish each cluster center with a few Newton steps on the real cubic
false: Report the cluster means, since the surrogate already agrees to two figures
Refit with more and more components until the liquid root finally matches
Discard the liquid root as an artifact of sampling a narrow region

items.context:
Z was sampled uniformly on [0.01, 0.99] and a 12-component mixture was fitted to (Z, r).
The vapor and unstable roots come out within 1%, but the liquid root is 26% high. Which
change fixes it in the course's fit?
items.why:
The liquid root sits in a narrow region where the cubic changes quickly, so the fit there is
sensitive to choices such as K, scaling and seed. Fitting in log Z gives that region more
resolution, and the liquid root comes out at 0.0346 against 0.0348. The paper's own fit
reached 0.035 without it, so this is one fix among several.
items.true: Fit in log Z, which spreads out the small values of Z
false: Use fewer components, so that each one covers more of the data
Condition on r = 0.001 instead of r = 0, to stay clear of the root
Sample Z more coarsely, so that the cubic looks smoother to EM

items.context:
For the same job, how does the data a generative model of p(x, y) needs compare with what a
regression of y on x needs?
items.why:
A regression models how y depends on x. A model of the joint does that and also models the
distribution of x, which is extra work paid for in samples, and density estimation gets
harder fast as the dimension grows. Generated samples are not new data.
items.true: More, because it also has to model how x is distributed
false: Less, because sampling creates new training data
The same, because both see the same rows
Less, because a mixture has fewer parameters than a network

items.context:
You condition a generative model on a value far outside its training data. What do you
get?
items.why:
Nothing in the sampling step checks whether the condition is supported by data. The
notebook asks about the gap in the |x| data and both models answer; the mixture is close to
right only because its straight ellipses extend straight branches.
items.true: Samples, with no warning, shaped by how the model behaves off the data
false: An error, because the condition has zero probability under the model
The single nearest training point, returned exactly and every time
Samples from the unconditional distribution, with the condition ignored

items.context:
A generative model trained on a plant's historian data proposes an optimal operating point.
Which statement is fair?
items.why:
A generative model is a surrogate of the data. Its samples satisfy the learned
distribution, not necessarily the plant, and it learns the plant as it was operated, so the
true optimum may be somewhere the data never went. Tight samples show the surrogate is
confident, not that it is right.
items.true: It solves the surrogate, which only knows the regions the plant has operated in
false: It is optimal for the plant, because every row of the data came from that plant
It is guaranteed feasible, because the operators always kept the plant feasible
It is certified optimal as long as the generated samples are tightly clustered

items.context:
"MatterGen designed a material and the lab measured its property within 20% of the
target." The target bulk modulus was 200 GPa. What does the paper's measurement actually
support?
items.why:
The bulk modulus was estimated from nanoindentation as "up to 169 GPa after four
measurements (158 ± 11 GPa)". 169 GPa is the upper end of that range and is within 20% of
200 GPa; the central value, 158 GPa, is 21% below. Only one of the four candidates chosen
for synthesis was made, and DFT on the ordered structure gave 222 GPa.
items.true: 158 ± 11 GPa: within 20% only at the top of the range, 21% below at its center
false: A central estimate within 5% of the target, from four direct measurements
Agreement between DFT and the experiment at 222 GPa, well within the 20%
All four synthesized candidates landing within 20% of their own targets

items.context:
Across the survey (proteins, materials, weather, process engineering), what do the
successful uses of generative models have in common?
items.why:
RFdiffusion's designs were characterized in the laboratory, MatterGen's candidate was
synthesized and measured, GenCast was scored against a held-out year of weather, and the
evaporator samples were checked against the process equations.
items.true: The generator proposes, and a lab or a physical model verifies
false: They were trained on more data than any discriminative model in their field
They replaced the physical model of the system entirely, once trained
Their samples were valid by construction and needed no further checks

items.context: Carlini et al. generated 175 million images from Stable Diffusion. What did they find?
items.why:
From 500 generations for each of 350,000 heavily duplicated training captions, 94 images
met their definition of extraction, and manual inspection found 13 more near-copies. Rare,
and real: a model trained on proprietary records can leak them.
items.true: 94 generated images counted as extracted training images
false: No generated image matched any image in the training set
About half of the generated images were copies of training images
Copies appeared only when a prompt explicitly asked for a known image
